intro:
These exercises move profiling out of a single process and into the spaces between processes. The recurring theme is that "slow" stops being one number once work travels through brokers, leases, worker pools, and reducers: the latency a user feels is the sum of queue wait, worker execution, retries, and fan-out, and each segment needs its own signal. The drills ask you to design that signal set deliberately, read an incident across logs, metrics, and traces, and compute the headline numbers an operator should see before the page fills with guesses.

The lab and the implementation exercise are the same shape as the chapter's first example: fold one profiling window down to worker saturation, retry rate, and an explicit storm flag. The later exercises push toward graph-aware profiling (critical path instead of stage-local averages) and capacity planning that includes replay traffic and drain time rather than only happy-path throughput. Throughout, the editorial rule is the same one the chapter states: handler CPU is usually not the system; queue age, retries, and fan-in often are.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design metrics for worker saturation
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The three pools answer different questions, so they need overlapping but distinct metric sets. The shared backbone is the same for all of them, and matches the chapter's three-shape rule: counters answer "how much happened," gauges answer "what is the level right now," and histograms answer "what is the distribution."

Counters (monotonic, per pool): tasks_admitted_total (admission), tasks_completed_total and tasks_failed_total (completion outcome), tasks_retried_total (replay load, not just failures), and dedupe_suppressed_total (duplicates dropped by idempotency). Admission minus completion over a window already hints at backlog; retried over claimed is the retry rate that the storm rule keys on.

Gauges (instantaneous level, per pool): queue_depth (visible backlog), in_flight (claimed-but-not-done work), and oldest_message_age_seconds. Oldest visible age is the one to watch hardest — it is a better operational target than average depth because a single stuck partition shows up there while the average still looks calm.

Histograms (distribution, per pool): queue_wait_seconds (time before claim), run_seconds (handler execution), and end_to_end_seconds (admission to durable completion). The split is what lets you separate worker saturation from queue saturation: worker saturation is busy_workers / total_workers near 1.0 with a healthy queue_wait; queue saturation is a rising queue_wait and oldest_message_age while run_seconds stays flat. The GPU pool will lean on run_seconds and in_flight; the reducer pool needs oldest_message_age and queue_depth most, because fan-in is where backlog hides.

Forbidden labels: never attach task_id or trace_id to a metric — those are unbounded and produce one time series per task, which is the classic cardinality explosion. Per-task identity belongs in logs and traces, where you can pivot on it; metrics should carry only low-cardinality dimensions such as pool name, queue name, and outcome.
criteria: Includes counters (admitted/completed/retried/dedupe), gauges (queue_depth, in_flight, oldest_message_age), and histograms (queue_wait, run, end_to_end), each with a stated reason.
Distinguishes worker saturation (busy/total near 1.0 with healthy queue wait) from queue saturation (rising queue wait and oldest age while run time is flat).
Names task_id and trace_id as forbidden labels because they are unbounded and explode cardinality.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace a tail-latency incident across logs, metrics, and traces
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The dominant layer is not the handler. The trace splits the 970 ms of observed time into 900 ms before claim and 70 ms inside the handler, so roughly 93 percent of end-to-end time is queue wait, plus the replay overhead of two failed attempts before success. Handler p50 being flat is exactly the trap the chapter warns about: when end-to-end latency rises while run time stays flat, the time is being spent before the handler, not inside it. Optimizing handler CPU here would move p99 by tens of milliseconds against a 900 ms wait — it cannot fix the incident.

The metric that should have alerted earlier than handler p50 is queue wait (queue_wait p95) or, equivalently, oldest_message_age. Both rise as soon as work starts waiting for a free worker, minutes before any handler-time metric moves. A retry-rate counter would also have flagged the replay component early.

To make the retry path attributable to one task you need stable identity carried in the envelope and echoed into logs and trace events: task_id (the same value across all three attempts) and attempt (1, 2, 3, so you can separate the first try from the redeliveries), plus queue_name so multi-queue tail analysis is possible. With task_id you can collapse the three log lines into one story; with attempt you can confirm the first two were timeouts, not genuine handler failures.

The first mitigation to test targets the real bottleneck, which is queueing plus replay amplification — not handler CPU. Options, cheapest first: raise the worker budget for that pool (more concurrent claims drains the backlog), cap or back off retries so failed attempts stop adding to arrival rate, or split the slow class onto its own queue so it stops blocking fast work. Increasing the worker budget or capping retries is the change to try before touching handler code.
criteria: Identifies queue wait (900 ms) plus replay, not handler CPU (70 ms), as the dominant layer.
Names queue_wait p95 / oldest_message_age as the earlier metric and task_id plus attempt as the identity fields that make the incident explainable.
Proposes a mitigation tied to the bottleneck (raise worker budget, cap retries, or split the queue) rather than optimizing the handler.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement a retry-storm window summary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This is a metric-and-policy drill, not a transport drill, so the whole point is to keep the helpers side-effect free and make the threshold logic visible in code. Each helper is a pure reduction over one WindowStats sample.

Saturation is busy_workers / total_workers cast to f64, guarded against a zero pool so it returns 0.0 instead of NaN. Retry rate is retried / claimed, guarded the same way against an empty window. Both are simple ratios, which is the property that makes them reviewable and testable.

The storm rule is the part that must not hide in prose. Encode the two thresholds as named constants and make retry_storm a single boolean expression: saturation at or above the saturation threshold AND retry rate at or above the retry threshold. Requiring both is deliberate — high saturation alone can be healthy throughput, and a high retry rate on an idle pool is not yet a storm. It is the combination, the feedback loop of saturation causing timeouts causing retries causing more load, that the flag is meant to catch. With claimed=100, retried=40, busy=9, total=10 the sample yields saturation 0.90, retry rate 0.40, and storm true, because 0.90 >= 0.85 and 0.40 >= 0.30.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Pure reductions over one window; the storm policy is two named thresholds combined with AND.
criteria: saturation = busy/total and retry_rate = retried/claimed are computed correctly, with zero-guards to avoid division by zero.
The storm rule is an explicit boolean over two named threshold constants, not buried in prose.
When you implement the three helpers, running the program prints saturation = 0.90, retry rate = 0.40, and storm = true.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a profiling surface that hides queue latency
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that the system instruments only the handler. Handler spans tell you run time, which is the one segment that already looks fine; the missing segment is everything before claim, so queue wait is invisible and backlog cannot be explained. The fix is to record the boundary timestamps and carry the correlation identity through the envelope.

Timestamps: stamp enqueued_at when the producer puts the task on the broker and claimed_at when a worker leases it. Queue wait is then claimed_at minus enqueued_at, and it can be computed without a dedicated span. The handler already gives you started_at and finished_at for run time. Carry these in the task envelope alongside the identity fields so the worker side has the producer-side timestamp available.

Log fields that must appear on both the enqueue side and the worker side: task_id and trace_id (stable across the whole trip and across retries), queue_name (without it, multi-queue tail analysis is nearly impossible), and attempt (separates first try from redeliveries). The enqueue-side log records the submission; the worker-side log records claim and completion; sharing task_id and trace_id is what stitches them into one record.

Model queue wait as derived time between two events (enqueued_at and claimed_at), not as a separate always-on span. The two events are cheap to stamp and the subtraction is free at query time, whereas a dedicated queue span adds an exporter write on every single task. For cost control on the hot path, keep aggregate metrics at full volume — a queue_wait histogram and oldest_message_age gauge are cheap and always-on — and attach full detailed traces only on a sampled fraction (plus always-sample on error or on tasks over a latency threshold). That gives you the population view from metrics and enough exemplars to explain one incident path without paying for a span per task.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Derive queue wait from enqueued_at/claimed_at rather than a per-task span; carry task_id, trace_id, queue_name, attempt for correlation.
criteria: Adds enqueue and claim visibility explicitly via enqueued_at and claimed_at, exposing queue wait that handler spans alone hide.
Includes stable correlation fields (task_id and trace_id) present on both the enqueue side and the worker side.
Names a cost-control tactic: full-volume aggregate metrics plus sampled (and error-triggered) detailed traces, with queue wait derived rather than spanned.

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile a task graph by critical path instead of average stage time
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is treating end-to-end time as the sum of stage averages. In a DAG, parallel stages overlap, so summing their durations double-counts time the system never spent, and a per-stage average can look healthy while the graph is globally slow. The signal that actually predicts completion is the critical path: the longest dependency chain when each node's cost is its own queue wait plus run time added to the maximum finishing time among its parents. Add all three graph-aware signals — critical-path time as the headline, frontier (in-flight node) size to spot fan-out width blowing up the pool, and reducer backlog to spot fan-in stalls — but critical path is the first honest simplification.

Queue wait belongs inside the graph accounting, not outside it. Each node's contribution is queue_ms + run_ms, exactly as the chapter's Example 2 computes; if you fold queue time into a separate global number, a join that is slow purely because its inputs sat in a queue will be misattributed to the worker. Keeping wait per node is what makes the critical path honest. The longest-path walk has one silent invariant: stages must appear in topological order, so that every dependency index is strictly smaller than the dependent stage's index. If a node references a dependency with a higher index, it reads a not-yet-computed (zero) slot and undercounts the critical path; in production, sort the stages first or compute the order before walking.

To prove a join stage is the real bottleneck rather than one upstream worker, walk the critical path and check where the longest finishing time is realized. If the join's predecessors all finish early but the join's own queue_ms (it waited for a free reducer) or the max-over-parents term dominates, the bottleneck is fan-in, not a single upstream stage. The tail-stage name returned by the critical-path computation tells you which node sits at the end of the longest path; if it is consistently the join, that is your proof.

For attribution under fan-out and fan-in, carry parent_task_id (and the root trace_id) in every envelope so children can be reassembled into the parent graph, and sample whole traces by root rather than by individual span — otherwise a fan-out of width 200 gives you 200 disconnected fragments. Sampling by root keeps the graph story attributable: you either get the entire DAG for a sampled job or none of it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Critical path with per-node queue+run cost; the returned tail names the stage at the end of the longest path. Stages must be ordered so that every dependency index is strictly smaller than the dependent stage's index (topological order); otherwise a node reads a not-yet-computed parent and the answer is wrong.
criteria: Adds a graph-aware signal (critical-path time, plus frontier size and reducer backlog) beyond per-stage averages.
Keeps queue wait inside the graph by making each node's cost queue_ms + run_ms rather than a separate global number.
Proposes attribution via parent_task_id / root trace_id and sampling whole traces by root for fan-out and fan-in nodes.

exerciseSolutions.title: Capacity-plan a distributed worker fleet with retries and slow-stage isolation
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Design the pipeline ingest -> parse -> enrich -> store -> notify as separate stages with separate budgets, because a single global budget lets the one long-running stage starve everything else. The stage that deserves its own queue and worker pool is the long-running specialist (call it enrich). With one shared pool, slow enrich tasks hold workers while fast parse and notify tasks queue behind them; isolating it bounds head-of-line blocking and lets you scale it independently to meet the oldest-age budget.

Size each pool from arrival rate and service time, then inflate for replay. By Little's Law the in-flight work for a stage is arrival_rate x service_time, and the worker count needed is roughly arrival_rate x service_time targeted below the queueing cliff (do not plan a stage at 100 percent utilization — keep it around 70 to 80 percent so a small burst does not push oldest-age past 2 s). Retry traffic is not rare noise: it adds to arrival rate. If the failure profile is f (fraction of tasks that fail and redeliver), effective arrival is roughly arrival / (1 - f) for at-least-once delivery, so a 10 percent failure rate is about 11 percent more load, and a storm can be far worse. Plan the worker budget against the effective, replay-inflated arrival rate, not the submission rate of 180/s alone.

The metrics that warn the 2-second oldest-age budget is about to fail are, in order: oldest_message_age_seconds (the direct target), queue_wait p95, worker_saturation (busy/total approaching 1.0), and retry_rate. Watching oldest age plus saturation plus retry rate plus reducer/enrich backlog gives minutes of warning before the budget breaks, because those four move before the budget itself does.

Finally, put a drain target in the same plan: on shutdown or deploy, stop admitting new work and require the fleet to drain in-flight and queued tasks within a bounded window (for example, drain to oldest-age 0 within 30 seconds). Drain time is governed by backlog size divided by completion rate, so it is the same capacity arithmetic — a fleet sized only for steady-state throughput can have a drain time far longer than its lease timeout, which causes duplicate processing on restart.
criteria: Isolates the long-running specialist stage (enrich) onto its own queue and pool to prevent head-of-line blocking.
Includes retries in the budget by planning against replay-inflated effective arrival (arrival / (1 - failure_fraction)), not the raw 180/s.
Names at least three observability hooks: oldest_message_age, worker saturation, retry rate, and stage/reducer backlog.
Adds a drain/shutdown target (bounded drain within a window) alongside steady-state throughput, tied to the same capacity arithmetic.

labSolution.explanation:
Each helper is a pure reduction over one WindowStats window, which keeps the lab trivial to test: no I/O, no shared state, no transport. saturation divides busy_workers by total_workers, guarded against a zero pool so it returns 0.0 rather than NaN; retry_rate divides retried by claimed with the same guard. Both take &WindowStats by shared reference, so the caller keeps ownership and the same sample can be read by every helper without a clone.

The storm policy is deliberately not hidden in prose. Two named constants, SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD (0.85) and RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD (0.30), make the thresholds reviewable, and retry_storm is a single boolean expression requiring both to be met. The AND matters: high saturation alone can be healthy throughput, and a high retry rate on an idle pool is not yet a storm; it is the combination — the feedback loop of saturation causing timeouts causing retries causing more load — that the flag catches.

For the sample (claimed 100, retried 40, busy 9, total 10), saturation is 9/10 = 0.90, retry rate is 40/100 = 0.40, and the storm flag is true because 0.90 >= 0.85 and 0.40 >= 0.30. The {:.2} format specifier prints both ratios to two decimals, producing exactly the expected three lines.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is queue latency often a better first incident signal than mean handler time?
reviewAnswers.answer: End-to-end latency is the sum of queue wait, run time, and replay, and when work backs up the time accumulates before the handler ever runs. Mean handler time stays flat in exactly that situation, so it cannot page you, whereas queue wait (or oldest visible age) rises the instant work starts waiting for a free worker. The chapter's rule is that if end-to-end latency rises while run time is flat, the cost is before the handler, not inside it — so queue latency moves earlier and points at the real layer.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes a retry storm a load-amplification problem instead of only an error-rate problem?
reviewAnswers.answer: A retry storm is a feedback loop: failures cause redeliveries, redeliveries add to the arrival rate, the higher arrival pushes workers past saturation, saturation causes more timeouts, and the timeouts produce still more retries. So retries are load, not just failure bookkeeping — every redelivery is another claim competing for the same workers. Treating it as only an error-rate problem misses that the system can be amplifying its own traffic until the queue and oldest-age signals climb out of control.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should task ID and trace ID stay out of metric labels but stay present in logs and traces?
reviewAnswers.answer: Task ID and trace ID are effectively unbounded, so attaching them as metric labels creates one time series per task and explodes cardinality, which can overwhelm the metrics backend. Metrics should carry only low-cardinality dimensions like pool name, queue name, and outcome, which still aggregate cleanly. Logs and traces are where per-task identity belongs: there you pivot on a single task_id or trace_id to reconstruct one incident path, including separating the first attempt from its retries.

reviewAnswers.question: What does critical-path time explain that stage-local averages do not explain?
reviewAnswers.answer: In a DAG, parallel stages overlap, so summing stage durations double-counts time the system never spent and a per-stage average can look healthy while the graph is globally slow. Critical-path time is the longest dependency chain, where each node's cost is its own queue wait plus run time added to the maximum finishing time among its parents — that is the number that actually predicts completion. It exposes reducer lag and join bottlenecks, because a fan-in node can sit on the longest path purely from waiting on its slowest input even when every stage's average is fine.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should capacity planning include drain time and retry traffic, not only steady-state throughput?
reviewAnswers.answer: Retries inflate the effective arrival rate (roughly arrival / (1 - failure fraction) under at-least-once delivery), so planning on happy-path throughput underestimates the real worker budget and the pool tips over the queueing cliff sooner than expected. Drain time matters because on shutdown or deploy the fleet must clear in-flight and queued work within a bounded window; a fleet sized only for steady state can have a drain time longer than its lease timeout, which causes duplicate processing on restart. Both are the same Little's-Law arithmetic applied to replay-inflated load and to backlog over completion rate.
